# Review pack: review-twelve-factor

Everything a worker needs for this skill, in one file: `SKILL.md`, `references/checklist.md`, the skill's other reference files and its language-neutral standards. Language-specific standards and signals are in `packs/review-twelve-factor.<language>.md`. Where the instructions below say to load one of these files, use its section here instead; don't open the original. Citation columns (anchors, pages, source names) are left out: cite an element by its ID in `Finding.element` and the report script fills in `standard` and `url`. `sources.md` is maintainer material and is not included.

## File: `SKILL.md`

### Review: Twelve-Factor App

Assesses whether each deployable is built to run as a twelve-factor app: one codebase, declared and isolated
dependencies, config outside the code, backing services as attached resources, separated build/release/run stages,
stateless and disposable processes, port binding, process-model scaling, dev/prod parity, logs as event streams and
one-off admin processes. Modern platform equivalents (container images, orchestrator-injected config, secret
managers, OTLP exporters) count when they meet a factor's intent.

#### Inputs

The capped file list assigned by `compliance-inventory` (config files including environment-named ones, `Dockerfile`,
`docker-compose*.yml`, process and workload definitions, entry point and startup files, logging configuration,
dependency manifests, `.env.example`, admin or migration script locations), plus the header value `targetGitHead`.
Review only those files.

#### Standards (local, authoritative)

- `references/standards/twelve-factor-app.md`: TFA-01…TFA-55, summarized from 12factor.net. Always load.
- `references/standards/twelve-factor-rubric.md`: TFR-01…TFR-20, the applicability table and accepted modern
  equivalents. Always load.
- Do **not** fetch any URL for this skill. Do not load `references/standards/MAINTENANCE.md`.
- If no element covers a situation, apply the closest element if it clearly fits. Otherwise mark the check N/A
  ("not covered by localized standard") and add `localized-standard-gap: <description>` to `notes`.

#### Procedure

1. Load `references/checklist.md`, `references/sources.md` and both standards files.
2. Skip generated and vendored files (`obj/`, `bin/`, `target/`, `build/`, `dist/`, `node_modules/`, `vendor/`);
   read lock files only to confirm a declaration exists. Note any skipped.
3. Classify each deployable with the rubric's applicability table and mark excluded checks N/A
   ("not applicable to <kind>"). A check fails if any deployable in the file list fails it; name the deployable.
   If the kind is unclear, treat it as a long-running service, use confidence `low` for kind-dependent findings and
   add `localized-standard-gap: deployable kind unclear` to `notes`.
4. Modern equivalents listed in the rubric satisfy an element. Fail only on a concrete rubric fail signal in the
   reviewed files. If the comparison partner isn't visible (e.g. no production backing-service definition for TF-10,
   no Dockerfile, manifest or deploy step for TF-05), mark the check N/A ("<what> not visible"). Development-gated
   configuration passes everywhere except TF-10.
5. TF-01: version control is shown by a non-null `targetGitHead` or a `.hg/`/`.svn/` directory at the root; never
   read Git data, and never fail TF-01 because version control isn't visible (mark TFA-01 N/A instead).
6. For each check TF-01…TF-12, evaluate only the elements it lists whose "Applies when" condition holds; if none
   apply, mark the check N/A with that reason.
7. Boundaries: don't fail for lock files or version pinning (review-dependency-management), secret delivery hygiene
   or log-file protection (review-security-operational; hardcoded credentials fail TF-03 *and* SEC-OP-05 on purpose),
   log structure, telemetry export or health endpoints (review-observability), message ack, requeue or idempotency
   (review-reliability), scale-out efficiency other than statelessness (review-performance; statelessness, session state and sticky sessions are judged only here, TF-06), release automation, SemVer or committed binaries
   (review-software-lifecycle), config documentation (review-maintainability), or test-time substitutes
   (review-testing). TF-07 accepts TLS termination at a platform router; never recommend a plain-HTTP public listener.
8. Severity: every Finding takes the check's default severity from `checklist.md`;
   `checkResults.severityIfFailed` is always that default.
9. Citations: set `element` to the failed element's ID (e.g. `TFA-01`); the report script derives `standard` and `url`
   from it, so don't write them.
10. Note strengths where config is cleanly externalized with a documented template, images are built once and
    promoted, processes are stateless with graceful shutdown, or development mirrors production services.

#### Output

Labels: don't write `subject` or `subSubject`; the report script takes them from `references/checklist.md`
(the `Subject:` line and the check's `Sub-subject` column). Follow `compliance-review-core`'s `finding-schema.md`.

## File: `references/standards/twelve-factor-app.md`

*Load rule: TFA-01…TFA-55, summarized from 12factor.net. Always load.*

### The Twelve-Factor App (12factor.net) — localized summary

- Level: informational only; severity is the owning check's default.
- Reading rule: modern platform equivalents satisfy an element when they meet its intent (rubric TFR-06 and the
  "Accepted modern equivalents" column). The tool names on the pages (Capistrano, Foreman, Memcached, Vagrant, …) are
  examples, never requirements.
- The pages have **no section anchors** below the factor heading (both ids on each page point at its top). Citation:
  `Finding.url` = citation base + page path, e.g. `https://12factor.net/config`; the element ID in `Finding.standard`
  gives the precision.
- "Service-like" in *Applies when* means the rubric's applicability table doesn't exclude the check for the
  deployable's kind.

| ID | Requirement (summary) | Applies when | Check |
|---|---|---|---|
| TFA-01 | The app is tracked in a version control system. A codebase is one repo, or a set of repos sharing a root commit. | always | TF-01 |
| TFA-02 | One codebase per app. Several apps sharing the same code is a violation. Shared code is factored into libraries consumed through the dependency manager. | ≥ 2 deployables or shared code | TF-01 |
| TFA-03 | Several codebases form a distributed system. Each component is an app that complies with twelve-factor on its own. | multi-repo or multi-component system | TF-01 |
| TFA-04 | All deploys (production, staging, developer machines) run from the same codebase, possibly at different versions. There are no per-deploy copies of the code. | always | TF-01 |
| TFA-05 | The app never relies on implicitly present system-wide packages. It declares all dependencies, completely and exactly, in a manifest. | always | TF-02 |
| TFA-06 | A dependency isolation mechanism is used at run time, so no undeclared dependency leaks in from the surrounding system. | always | TF-02 |
| TFA-07 | Declaration and isolation are always used together. Either one alone is insufficient. | always | TF-02 |
| TFA-08 | The same full dependency specification applies to production and development. | always | TF-02 |
| TFA-09 | A new developer needs only the language runtime and the dependency manager. One deterministic build command sets up everything needed to run the code. | always | TF-02 |
| TFA-10 | The app doesn't rely on implicitly present system tools (for example by shelling out to an image tool or `curl`). Any tool it needs is vendored or declared. | app invokes external executables | TF-02 |
| TFA-11 | Config is everything that varies between deploys: handles to backing services, credentials to external services, and per-deploy values such as the canonical hostname. | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-12 | Config is strictly separated from code. Deploy-varying values are never stored as constants in the code. | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-13 | Litmus test: the codebase could be made open source at any moment without compromising any credential. | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-14 | Internal application config that doesn't vary between deploys (routing, module wiring) isn't "config" and belongs in the code. | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-15 | Config files kept out of version control are better than constants, but they are easy to commit by mistake, scatter across places and formats, and tie config to one language or framework. | config files used | TF-03 |
| TFA-16 | Config is supplied through environment variables, a language- and OS-agnostic mechanism that changes per deploy without code changes. Platform equivalents count (TFR-06). | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-17 | Config values are granular, independent controls managed per deploy. They aren't batched into named environment groups (development, test, production), which multiply as deploys grow. | service-like | TF-03 |
| TFA-18 | A backing service is anything the app consumes over the network: datastores, queues, mail, caches, metrics and third-party APIs. | backing services used | TF-04 |
| TFA-19 | The code doesn't distinguish local from third-party services. Both are attached resources reached through a URL or locator plus credentials held in config. | backing services used | TF-04 |
| TFA-20 | Swapping a resource (for example a local database for a managed one, or a mail server for a provider) needs only a config change, no code change. | backing services used | TF-04 |
| TFA-21 | Each distinct backing service is its own resource with its own handle. Two databases are two resources. | ≥ 2 instances of a service type | TF-04 |
| TFA-22 | Resources attach to and detach from a deploy at will, without code changes. They are loosely coupled. | backing services used | TF-04 |
| TFA-23 | The build stage turns a specific commit into an executable bundle: it fetches or vendors dependencies and compiles binaries and assets. | service-like | TF-05 |
| TFA-24 | The release stage combines a build with the deploy's current config into a release ready to execute. | service-like | TF-05 |
| TFA-25 | The run stage launches the app's processes against one selected release. | service-like | TF-05 |
| TFA-26 | Build, release and run are strictly separated. Code can't be changed at run time. | service-like | TF-05 |
| TFA-27 | Every release has a unique ID (a timestamp or an incrementing number). Releases are an append-only ledger and are never changed after creation. Any change creates a new release. | deployment config visible | TF-05 |
| TFA-28 | Release management makes it possible to roll back to a previous release. | deployment config visible | TF-05 |
| TFA-29 | The run stage has as few moving parts as possible. Complexity belongs in the build stage, where a developer sees the errors. | service-like | TF-05 |
| TFA-30 | Processes are stateless and share nothing. Any data that must persist is stored in a stateful backing service. | service-like | TF-06 |
| TFA-31 | Process memory or disk is used only as a brief, single-transaction cache. The app never assumes such cached data is available to a later request or job. | service-like | TF-06 |
| TFA-32 | Assets are compiled in the build stage, not at run time into the process's filesystem. | app serves compiled assets | TF-06 |
| TFA-33 | No sticky sessions. Session state lives in a datastore with time-based expiry, never in process memory with affinity routing. | app has user sessions | TF-06 |
| TFA-34 | The app is self-contained. It doesn't rely on a web server injected at run time (an external servlet container or a server module), but exports HTTP by binding to a port itself. | network service | TF-07 |
| TFA-35 | The web server is a library added through dependency declaration and runs inside the app's own process. | network service | TF-07 |
| TFA-36 | The contract with the execution environment is binding to a port. A routing layer maps public hostnames to the port-bound processes. | network service | TF-07 |
| TFA-37 | Non-HTTP servers export their services by port binding too. One app can become another app's backing service through a URL in the consumer's config. | network service | TF-07 |
| TFA-38 | Each type of work is assigned to a process type (for example web and worker). The set of types and the count of each is the process formation. | service-like | TF-08 |
| TFA-39 | Internal threads or async are allowed, but the app also scales horizontally across processes and machines, not only vertically. | service-like | TF-08 |
| TFA-40 | Processes never daemonize or write PID files. The platform's process manager handles output streams, crash restarts and user-initiated restarts and shutdowns. | service-like | TF-08 |
| TFA-41 | Processes are disposable: they can be started or stopped at a moment's notice. | service-like | TF-09 |
| TFA-42 | Startup time is minimal, ideally a few seconds from launch until the process is ready for requests or jobs. | service-like | TF-09 |
| TFA-43 | On SIGTERM a web process shuts down gracefully: it stops listening, lets current requests finish, then exits. Requests are short, and long-polling clients reconnect. | network service | TF-09 |
| TFA-44 | The tools gap is small: development and production use stacks that are as similar as possible. | service-like | TF-10 |
| TFA-45 | The developer resists lightweight substitutes for backing services in development, even behind adapters. Small incompatibilities break code in production. Adapters are fine for porting, but not as a reason to diverge. | backing services used | TF-10 |
| TFA-46 | Every deploy (developer, staging, production) uses the same type and version of each backing service. | backing services used | TF-10 |
| TFA-47 | Local environments approximate production cheaply through packaged services, declarative provisioning and lightweight virtual environments (containers). | backing services used | TF-10 |
| TFA-48 | Logs are a time-ordered stream of events aggregated from the output of all processes, with no fixed beginning or end. A file is only one output format. | service-like | TF-11 |
| TFA-49 | The app never concerns itself with routing or storing its output stream. It doesn't write or manage log files. | service-like | TF-11 |
| TFA-50 | Each process writes its event stream, unbuffered, to stdout. | service-like | TF-11 |
| TFA-51 | The execution environment captures, collates and routes the streams to their destinations. Those destinations aren't visible to or configurable by the app. | service-like | TF-11 |
| TFA-52 | One-off admin tasks (database migrations, consoles, one-time scripts) run as one-off processes, separate from the regular process formation. | admin tasks exist | TF-12 |
| TFA-53 | One-off processes run in an environment identical to the regular processes: against a release, with the same codebase and config. | admin tasks exist | TF-12 |
| TFA-54 | Admin code ships with the application code, so the two can't drift out of sync. | admin tasks exist | TF-12 |
| TFA-55 | Every process type, admin processes included, uses the same dependency isolation and runtime invocation. | admin tasks exist | TF-12 |

## File: `references/standards/twelve-factor-rubric.md`

*Load rule: TFR-01…TFR-20, the applicability table and accepted modern equivalents. Always load.*

### Compliance Reviewer Twelve-Factor Rubric — local standard

- Level: every element is REVIEW (informational only); severity always comes from the owning check (SKILL.md).
- **Modern equivalents pass.** Anything listed under "Accepted modern equivalents" satisfies the element and the TFA
  elements of the same check. The tool names on the 12factor.net pages are examples, never requirements.
- **Fail only on a concrete fail signal** in the reviewed files, cited with file, lines and excerpt. If the comparison
  partner isn't visible, mark the check N/A ("<what> not visible"). Signals found only in development-gated
  configuration (a `Development` profile, `if DEBUG`, `docker-compose.override.yml`, a devcontainer) pass, except for
  TF-10, which compares development against production.
- An unknown framework: judge by intent where possible and add `localized-standard-gap: unknown framework <name>` to
  `notes` once.

#### Applicability by deployable kind (rules, not elements)

Classify each deployable in the file list. Mark the checks excluded for its kind N/A ("not applicable to <kind>").
When a repository holds several kinds, a check applies if any deployable kind in the file list keeps it, and a
finding names the deployable that fails. If the kind can't be determined, treat the deployable as a long-running
network service, use confidence `low` on kind-dependent findings and add
`localized-standard-gap: deployable kind unclear` to `notes`.

| Deployable kind | Recognized by (examples) | Checks N/A |
|---|---|---|
| Long-running network service (web, API, gRPC, socket) | Kestrel/ASP.NET host, Spring Boot web starter, gunicorn/uvicorn/Flask/Django/FastAPI app, Express/Fastify `listen`, `EXPOSE` in Dockerfile, a Service/Ingress for it | none |
| Worker / background consumer | Generic Host `BackgroundService`, `@KafkaListener`/`@RabbitListener`, Celery/RQ worker, queue consumer entry point, no listener | TF-07 |
| Scheduled job or CLI run in a deploy | K8s `CronJob`/`Job`, cron schedule, console `Main` with args, `click`/`argparse` entry point | TF-07, TF-08 |
| Local stdio MCP server (a subprocess its MCP client launches) | MCP SDK with a stdio transport only (`WithStdioServerTransport`, `StdioServerTransportProvider`, `run()`/`run("stdio")`), no HTTP listener | TF-07, TF-08. For TF-11, `stdout` is the protocol channel, so a log event stream to `stderr` satisfies the factor; logs on `stdout` are judged by `review-mcp-server` MCP-01, not here |
| Serverless function | `host.json`/`function.json`, `serverless.yml`, SAM/`template.yaml` handlers, `@app.function_name`, Lambda handler | TF-07, TF-08, TF-09 (the platform owns process lifecycle) |
| Static front end (SPA or static site with no server of its own) | `package.json` build to `dist/`/`build/`, no server entry point | TF-04, TF-06, TF-07, TF-08, TF-09, TF-11, TF-12 |
| Library or package (no deployable entry point) | publishable package metadata (`<PackageId>`/`IsPackable`, `<packaging>jar</packaging>` without a main, `pyproject` without scripts, `package.json` `main`/`exports` only) | TF-03 … TF-12 |
| Desktop or mobile client | WinForms/WPF/MAUI/Avalonia, Android/iOS project files, Electron | TF-03 … TF-12 |

#### Elements

| ID | Check | Requirement and pass criterion | Accepted modern equivalents | Fail signals (in reviewed files) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TFR-01 | TF-01 | Version control is shown by `targetGitHead` ≠ `null`, or by a `.hg/`/`.svn/` directory at the root. Otherwise TFA-01 is N/A ("version control not visible: target may be an export"), never failed. Never read Git data. | Any VCS | none for TFA-01 |
| TFR-02 | TF-01 | One codebase per app: deployables share code through project, module or package references, never through copied source. Deploys differ only in config. | Monorepo with `ProjectReference`, Maven/Gradle modules, workspace packages, internal package feed | the same source files duplicated across deployables; per-deploy code copies (`src-prod/`, `app-staging/`, `*-prod` forks); build scripts that pick different source trees per environment |
| TFR-03 | TF-02 | Every dependency the reviewed entry points and config use is declared in the deployable's manifest. Lock files aren't judged (DEP-02). | `PackageReference`/central package management, `pom.xml`/`build.gradle`, `pyproject.toml`/`requirements*.txt`, `package.json` | no manifest for a deployable; imports of packages not declared; `<Reference HintPath>` or `sys.path`/`PYTHONPATH` pointing at machine paths; GAC or site-packages assumptions |
| TFR-04 | TF-02 | Dependencies are isolated at run time, the same way in development and production. | Container image built from the manifest; virtualenv/Poetry/uv; per-project NuGet/Maven resolution; `node_modules` per project; self-contained publish | setup docs or scripts needing global installs for runtime deps (`npm install -g`, `sudo pip install`, `pip install` outside an image or venv); production Dockerfile installing different packages from those the manifest declares |
| TFR-05 | TF-02 | Executables the app invokes are provided by the repo (installed with a version in the Dockerfile, declared in a manifest, or vendored). | `apt-get install <tool>=<version>` in the Dockerfile; tool as a package dependency | `Process.Start`/`subprocess`/`Runtime.exec`/`child_process` calling a tool (for example ImageMagick, `wkhtmltopdf`, `ffmpeg`, `curl`) that nothing in the repo provides |
| TFR-06 | TF-03 | Deploy-varying values reach the app from the deploy, never from the code. *(Pass criterion.)* | Env vars; K8s ConfigMap/Secret env or file mounts; Docker/compose secrets; Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, HashiCorp Vault, Azure App Configuration, Spring Cloud Config, located through env or platform identity; committed defaults that are local-development values only (localhost, password-less) and overridable by env | — (pass criterion) |
| TFR-07 | TF-03 | No deploy-varying value is hardcoded. | — | hosts, URLs, connection strings, credentials, canonical hostnames, bucket or queue names, or account IDs as literals in code, or in committed config without an override path; code branching on the environment name to pick such values (`if env == "prod": url = …`); a compose or workload file with literal production values (secrets there are also SEC-OP-05, on purpose) |
| TFR-08 | TF-03 | Environment-named config files hold no deploy-specific values. | Environment-named files with behavior settings only (log levels, feature defaults identical for every deploy of that kind) pass, with an optional `notes` remark | `appsettings.<Env>.json`, `application-<profile>.yml`, `settings/production.py` or `config/<env>.js` containing production hosts, URLs, credentials or hostnames |
| TFR-09 | TF-04 | Every backing service is reached through a handle from config, and switching providers is a config change. | Connection strings or URLs bound from config; SDK clients built from endpoint config; provider chosen by a config value | hardcoded host, port or URL for a datastore, queue, cache, mail server or third-party API; provider implementation chosen by the environment name instead of config; a second resource's handle derived by editing the first one's string |
| TFR-10 | TF-05 | Nothing is built, installed or changed at run time, and deploy config isn't baked into the build. | Multi-stage Dockerfile; CI builds once and promotes the same artifact; config injected at release or deploy | entrypoint or start script running `npm install`, `pip install`, `dotnet build`/`dotnet run`, `mvn package`, `git pull` or asset compilation; `npm run dev` or a development server as the production command; deploy-specific config or secrets copied or `ARG`-passed into the image |
| TFR-11 | TF-05 | Deployments reference a unique, immutable release ID, so rollback means redeploying an earlier ID. | Image tag or digest with commit SHA, build number or version; Helm revision; platform release IDs | deployment manifests or deploy steps referencing only `:latest` or another mutable tag; a deploy step that overwrites the running artifact in place |
| TFR-12 | TF-06 | Session and user state live in a backing store, and no routing affinity is needed. | Distributed session stores (Redis, SQL, Spring Session); stateless tokens; in-memory caches holding re-derivable data | in-memory session providers in a service deployed with more than one instance or with autoscale (`AddDistributedMemoryCache` + `AddSession`, express-session `MemoryStore`, servlet `HttpSession` without an external store, Flask filesystem sessions); session-affinity settings (ARR affinity, `sessionAffinity: ClientIP`, ingress cookie affinity) |
| TFR-13 | TF-06 | Process-local disk is scratch only. | Uploads and generated files written to blob or object storage or a database; `emptyDir`/tmp for one request | user uploads, generated reports or job state written to a local path that later requests read; in-memory static collections or job queues treated as the source of truth |
| TFR-14 | TF-07 | Network services host their own listener and take the port from the environment or a fixed container port. TLS may end at a platform router; never recommend a plain-HTTP public listener. | Kestrel, embedded Tomcat/Jetty/Netty (Spring Boot jar), gunicorn/uvicorn, Node `listen(process.env.PORT)`, fixed `EXPOSE` with platform port mapping | WAR or EAR deployed into an external servlet container; app only runs as a module or in-process inside an external web server (for example IIS in-process hosting with no self-host path); no listener in a service that is otherwise network-facing |
| TFR-15 | TF-08 | Each process type runs as its own platform-managed process, scaled by count, and processes stay in the foreground. | Procfile entries, separate compose services or K8s workloads per process type, hosted worker services, replica counts or autoscalers | daemonizing (`daemon = True`, `nohup … &`, `start-stop-daemon`, `--daemon`); PID files; one container running several process types under a shell `&` or an in-container supervisor; web and worker welded into one process with no way to scale either |
| TFR-16 | TF-09 | SIGTERM reaches the app and triggers a graceful shutdown. | Exec-form `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT`, `exec` in wrapper scripts, `tini`/`--init`; framework graceful shutdown (Generic Host, `server.shutdown=graceful`, gunicorn/uvicorn defaults, Node `SIGTERM` handler closing the server); a termination grace period longer than the drain time | shell-form `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` or wrapper scripts without `exec`, so the app isn't PID 1 and gets no signal; a Node or custom server with no `SIGTERM` handling while holding connections; a grace period set shorter than the configured shutdown timeout |
| TFR-17 | TF-09 | Startup does only what readiness needs, and it doesn't block on long one-off work. | Lazy warm-up; readiness probes; migrations as a release or one-off step (TF-12) | startup code that loads whole datasets, sleeps or retries for minutes before listening, or runs long migrations in every instance's startup path (confidence `medium` unless the cost is evident) |
| TFR-18 | TF-10 | Development configuration uses the same type and version of each backing service as production. Judge only when both sides are visible; otherwise N/A. | `docker-compose*.yml` or devcontainer services with the same images and major versions as production IaC or manifests; emulators of the same service (for example Azurite, LocalStack) | SQLite, H2, an in-memory EF provider or LocalDB in development while production uses PostgreSQL or SQL Server; in-memory cache or queue in development while production uses Redis or RabbitMQ; the same service at a different major version in compose and production |
| TFR-19 | TF-11 | Production logging writes to stdout/stderr. Any exporter takes its destination from the environment. | Console sinks or appenders; JSON to stdout; OTLP or collector exporter with endpoint from env (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`); file sinks only in development-gated config | file appenders or sinks, rotation settings or log paths in production config (`RollingFileAppender`, Serilog File sink, NLog file target, Python `FileHandler`/`RotatingFileHandler`, winston File transport); a hardcoded log-shipping destination in the app; logs written only to a file inside the container. Buffered stdout (for example Python without `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`) is a recommendation, not a failure. |
| TFR-20 | TF-12 | Admin tasks are committed with the app and run from the same release, image and config as the app. | Migration tools in the repo run as a K8s `Job` or init container from the same image, `docker compose run <app> <task>`, a Procfile `release:` phase, or a CI or CD step using the built artifact | admin or migration scripts kept outside the repo or referenced by a path on a server; admin tasks needing a different runtime, dependency set or hand-installed tools; migrations applied by hand-run SQL with no runner. Migrations on every instance's startup are a TFR-17 concern and a recommendation here, not a TF-12 failure. |
